gaps.fact: Australia is about the size of the continental United States: no chapter, question or article gives the comparison or any measure of the continent's size.

The Court's two models, traditional (blending across regions in American oak) against modern (a single GI or site in French oak): the traditional half is asked (i-ly53hcj0, i-us7ohd88), but the move to single sites and French oak lives only in the barossa-eden and mclaren-vale articles; no chapter fact or question sets the two against each other.

The first vines of 1788 near Sydney, the industry's shift to South Australia behind its phylloxera quarantine, and fortified and sweet wine dominating until late in the twentieth century: the three dates are told only in the country overview; the bank asks the quarantine (i-49uu9qld) but never the year 1788, the shift or the fortified century.

The Yellow Tail business model (one inexpensive, consistent, fruit forward brand built for the American market) appears nowhere in the Codex, and the Australian purchase of the French business behind the Stelvin closure is never told: the bank names Stelvin only as a French brand from the 1970s trials (c-jralyu7t).

Opening and presenting a screw cap at the table: the Codex teaches the screwcap as a closure and its history (Wine Trade & Aging fact 6, c-jralyu7t, i-xy4ks8pu) but no SERVICE_REF table, chapter or question teaches the service itself. The same gap stands in New Zealand.

The Court's substitutions, Clare or Eden Riesling used like New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc, Yarra Pinot Noir alongside Willamette Valley Pinot Noir, Yarra Chardonnay alongside Sonoma Coast Chardonnay, appear nowhere; ripe Shiraz with grilled or barbecued meat lives only in article serving lines, never in a question.

notes: Mapped questions: Régionale 57 and Village 24 (Australia), 81 in all. Outside the mapped cats, i-q827d7lx, i-kytwa45i and i-xoboedyq (Producers & Icons), i-03zsquc8 and i-6q16l43f (Dessert & Sweet Wines), i-g6scztzh (Geography & Maps), c-2vk2rxzo (Terroir: Climate & Soil), c-5d2s2gyr and c-jmvrdnl2 (Sparkling Wine World) and i-4jkw2zst (Sparkling/Fortified/Sweet) touch Australia, and the nine regional articles carry their own questions (r- ids). The subject is the best served of the group: the crescent and its reasons, the Murray and Murrumbidgee bulk districts, the GI ladder with its homogeneity tests and the Coonawarra boundary case, the 85 per cent and descending order rules, the Label Integrity Program, the Old Vine Charter rungs, terra rossa, Hunter Semillon and Hunter River Riesling, Rutherglen's four steps and Topaque, Tasmania as one GI, Margaret River from the 1965 paper, and the Clare screwcap move of 2000. The thin cells are the continent's size, the modern French oak style, the 1788 and fortified history, Yellow Tail, the screw cap service and the Court's pairing substitutions. No factual error found: the 1842 Barossa settlement, Yarra 1838, Orange's height rule, the 1965 cask, the vine pull of the mid 1980s, the 70 year Survivor Vine rung, the Gin Gin clone, the Topaque change and the region test (five vineyards of five hectares, 500 tonnes) all hold. Court text notes, never altered: Penfold's Grange carries an apostrophe the house never uses (Penfolds); its Certified outcome reads will be know; its Introductory list puts Riverina and Murray Darling under South Eastern Australia, which is right (both are inside the super zone, Riverina in New South Wales, Murray Darling across the Victorian border). Two searches spent: new GI determinations since 2023 and the Tasmanian regions; no change found (Tasmania stays one GI with its seven informal areas, and Wilyabrup inside Margaret River was refused a final determination, as the country ladder already says of the Margaret River districts).
